title: Inside the Darién Gap
author: Belén Fernández
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/Screenshot-2026-06-27-at-10.30.36-AM-680x514.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/28/a-capurgana-
diary/)

_The following piece was funded by the[CounterPunch Investigative
Fund](https://www.counterpunch.org/397842-2/)._

Plastered onto the side of the glassed-in immigration office at the dock in
Necoclí – the northwestern Colombian city just across the Gulf of Urabá from
the [Darién Gap](https://www.rutgersuniversitypress.org/the-darien-
gap/9781978842083) – is a poster warning of the hazards of northbound
migration. Over recent years, more than [1.2 million](https://www.ap.org/news-
highlights/spotlights/2025/a-jungle-route-once-carried-hundreds-of-thousands-
of-migrants-now-the-local-economy-has-crashed/) people from a mind-boggling
[array of countries](https://www.csis.org/analysis/mind-darien-gap-migration-
bottleneck-americas) have risked their lives to cross the Gap, the
106-kilometer stretch of roadless territory and formidable jungle that spans
Colombia and Panama and constitutes the only land bridge between South and
Central America. Most of them hoped to reach the United States, the very
country that [makes much of the world
unlivable](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2025/12/31/here-is-to-a-quarter-
century-of-us-military-havoc) in the first place while simultaneously
criminalizing migration, thereby forcing the global have-nots down
increasingly lethal routes.

The protagonists of [the poster](https://www.instagram.com/p/DHJ3NwAK1fF/) are
the Díaz family – mom, dad, and two young daughters – whose portrait appears
superimposed over an image of a small boat packed with passengers. According
to the poster, which is in Spanish, _la familia_ Díaz had set out “in search
of a better future,” boarding just such a boat as they made their way toward
_los Estados Unidos_ : “Two days later, a rescue team found their lifeless
bodies, together with 59 other people who had also succumbed to the river’s
fury.”

When I last visited Necoclí in January, the sign had already lost its intended
audience. Hardly any migrants transit the Darién Gap these days, a result of
the decision by current gringo sociopath-in-chief Donald Trump to effectively
[shut down](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/01/fact-sheet-
president-donald-j-trump-protects-the-states-and-the-american-people-by-
closing-the-border-to-illegals-via-proclamation/) the US border with Mexico
and dispense with the concept of asylum. In the first three months of 2026,
for example, Panama recorded a total of [92
arrivals](https://www.migracion.gob.pa/wp-content/uploads/WEB-IRREGULARES-POR-
DARIEN-MARZO-2026.pdf) from Colombia via the jungle; in August 2023 alone,
there were [81,946](https://www.migracion.gob.pa/wp-
content/uploads/IRREGULARES-X-DARIEN-2023.pdf). I, however, certainly found
myself thinking a lot about _la familia_ Díaz over the two-hour course of a
high-speed, spine-shattering boat ride from Necoclí to the village of
Capurganá, which lies inside the Darién Gap and which, along with the nearby
village of Acandí, served as the principal points of departure for migrants
entering the jungle.

This was my second visit to Capurganá, the first having taken place in January
2024, when I, too, entered the jungle as a “migrant.” Like in 2024, I flew
into Medellín and took a nine-hour bus ride north to Necoclí, a gloriously
scenic trip that came with complimentary vomit bags, handed out by the bus
attendant for use on interminable mountain curves. Physically speaking, I was
better prepared for the continuous lurching this time around as I had taken an
uncharacteristic break from alcohol consumption, thanks to which I did not
even realize until my second day in Necoclí that the city had implemented _ley
seca_ , a temporary ban on alcohol sales. This was on account of recent tire-
burning and other local upheaval over the lands comprising the [Necoclí
hacienda](https://www.elcolombiano.com/antioquia/la-historia-de-la-virgen-del-
cobre-la-hacienda-que-tiene-prendida-a-uraba-KP32795780) Virgen del Cobre,
which had formerly been utilized by paramilitary and narco-trafficking outfits
and which the government of Gustavo Petro had undertaken to redistribute to
peasant victims of Colombia’s armed conflict.

One woman I spoke with in Necoclí suggested that _ley seca_ was one of the
reasons the city seemed like a ghost town, in the absence of the customary
ubiquitous music and alcohol-fueled ruckus. The other reason, of course, was
that the city was no longer brimming with migrants, who had filled hotels and
rental apartments, as well as the beach and sidewalks, for those who lacked
the money to put more than a tent, a cardboard box, or a hammock between
themselves and the elements. Every morning, the Necoclí dock became a vibrant
hub of activity as boat after boat departed for Acandí and Capurganá, with
vendors hawking arepas, waterproof cell phone pouches, rain ponchos, and
anything else the jungle-bound migrant might need. By January 2026, the
atmosphere was more subdued; most of the passengers on the Capurganá boat were
tourists from other parts of Colombia and Europe, who emitted synchronized
yelps as the vessel crashed against the waves.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/Screenshot-2026-06-27-at-10.29.50-AM-680x301.png)

Capurganá, image by Belén Fernández.

From the dock in Capurganá, a hamlet boasting intermittently turquoise waters
and no more than a few thousand inhabitants, migrants had been marched to
waiting auto rickshaws that transported them to the _albergue_ , or shelter.
This was the final stop before commencing the trek across the Darién Gap, a
trajectory that could take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks – for those
that survived the crossing, that is. The “shelter” was not so much a shelter
as a place for migrant smugglers to verify that all travelers were properly
extorted before being dispatched into the jungle in groups with guides, who
generally abandoned the migrants and turned back before even reaching the
border with Panama, leaving them vulnerable to robbery and sexual assault for
the remainder of the journey. [![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/Screenshot-2026-06-27-at-10.25.19-AM-680x918.png)](https://www.pilsencommunitybooks.com/item/BEN0A3pI11BCFh_dt7WwWA)

During my brief jungle incursion in 2024, I had also turned back with the
guide, owing in part to logistical considerations – such as that I had left my
computer behind in Necoclí – but mostly to the fact that I was too scared
shitless to brave the Darién Gap in its entirety. I was traveling with two
young Venezuelan men who had agreed to accompany me, and we had paid $280
apiece at the _albergue_ for what would ultimately be nine hours of walking:
five hours in the direction of Panama and four hours back, the quicker return
pace attributable to the diminished size of our group, which now no longer
included families with children. Our guide was a 28-year-old Afro-Colombian
woman with two children of her own; she was training to be a nurse, but had
jumped at the chance to earn some extra cash with the smuggling gig. As I had
revealed neither the journalistic nature of my Darién trip nor my US
citizenship, she was thoroughly baffled by my apparently spontaneous decision
to renounce the American dream and retreat to Capurganá. To her credit, she
refrained from asking too many questions and simply gave the two Venezuelans
her WhatsApp number in case they wanted to try the crossing again without me.

This year, on the other hand, I disembarked at the Capurganá dock and boarded
an auto rickshaw to a glamping establishment, as much as the term “glamping”
gave me an aneurysm every time I thought about it. There I would spend two
nights violating my personal _ley seca_ with wine made from the borojó fruit
and would make the acquaintance of an older woman from Bogotá who had lived in
the US for decades and was now attempting a vacation with her son amidst
unseasonal downpours. Having perfected the self-righteous entitlement of well-
heeled Colombians who had migrated to the US by plane rather than walking
through the Darién Gap, the woman lamented that today’s crop of migrants
simply devoted themselves to robbing drugstores and otherwise refusing to lead
respectable lives.

I had not come to Capurganá with any fixed plan aside from checking out the
post-migration panorama, but I had figured I might as well attempt to track
down a certain Darwin García Pérez, alias “Maradona,” who had been a key
coordinator of the trans-Darién migrant route. In a September 2023 _New York
Times_ [dispatch](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/09/14/world/americas/migrant-
business-darien-gap.html) titled “‘A Ticket to Disney’? Politicians Charge
Millions to Send Migrants to U.S.”, García was identified as an elected
community board member and one of the “entrepreneurs behind the migrant gold
rush,” who informed the _Times_ : “We have organized everything: the boatmen,
the guides, the bag carriers.” He was also quoted as declaring the deluge of
migrants to be “the best thing that could have happened” to a chronically poor
town, and had categorically denied affiliation with the Clan del Golfo,
Colombia’s most powerful drug trafficking organization, whose overarching
control of the migration enterprise was not exactly a secret. The same _Times_
article cited President Petro’s calculation that the Clan del Golfo was raking
in $30 million a year in its cut of the migratory proceeds – to say nothing of
the billions it accrued from drug running, [illegal gold
mining](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/26/world/americas/colombia-cartel-
illegal-gold-mining-military-base.html), and other pursuits. In October 2023,
the Colombian investigative news outlet _Vorágine_
[revealed](https://voragine.co/historias/reportaje/la-campana-politica-que-se-
lucra-con-la-plata-que-les-cobran-a-los-migrantes-en-el-darien/) that a
portion of the migration funds accumulated by Maradona and colleagues was
being funneled into the mayoral campaign of none other than Maradona’s half-
brother, Luis Fernando Martínez Pérez, who was duly elected that year.

Fast forward to January 2025, and the Colombian Fiscalía – or Attorney
General’s Office – [took to
X](https://x.com/FiscaliaCol/status/1883998360572490152) to announce migrant
trafficking and other charges against García, who was said to be the
proprietor and administrator of, inter alia, an _albergue_ and a maritime
transport company in the service of trafficking operations. The corresponding
[press release](https://www.fiscalia.gov.co/colombia/noticias/fiscalia-
judicializa-a-presunto-dinamizador-del-trafico-de-migrantes-en-uraba/)
specified that García was accused of collaboration with the Clan del Golfo and
of redirecting a percentage of migrant profits into the illicit outfit’s
coffers, which had resulted in his arrest in a “coordinated action” between
the Fiscalía, the Colombian National Police, the Colombian army’s Seventh
Brigade, and Colombian migration authorities.

Shortly after his dramatic capture, García was quietly
[released](https://caracol.com.co/2025/01/22/en-libertad-hermano-del-alcalde-
de-acandi-choco/), and I could find no further updates as to his subsequent
activities. While waiting for my boat to Capurganá at the dock in Necoclí, I
inquired about his alleged maritime transport company and received only
defiant assertions that he had never owned any such company. However, one
woman selling black garbage bags to passengers who did not wish to have their
belongings soaked had told me that García had passed through just days before,
meaning there was a good chance he was now in Capurganá. And so I set out from
the glamping site armed with my notebook and the silly conviction that it
would not only be a piece of cake to locate García but that he’d also be
thrilled to talk to me about whether he continued to consider migration “the
best thing that could have happened” to a village that despite substantial
migratory windfalls still lacked regular electricity and anything resembling a
health care system.[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/Screenshot-2026-06-27-at-10.40.59-AM.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/397842-2/)

My fantasies were quickly dispelled by my very first interlocutor, a resident
of Capurganá whom I’ll call Marcos. He said that of course he knew García, as
everyone knew everyone else in Capurganá, and did me the favor of calling him
right then and there on speakerphone to see if he might be up for a meeting.
García’s answer was clear: absolutely not. The _New York Times_ had distorted
his words, he said, and he had no interest in talking to journalists who were
simply out to smear his image. Marcos thanked him and hung up, then proceeded
to become visibly agitated: “Please don’t ask me any more questions, and
pretend we never had this conversation.” Upon hearing that I had envisioned
swinging by the _albergue_ -cum-migrant extortion center for old times’ sake,
he warned that such a visit would not go unperceived by the local powers that
be, and advised me for my own good to put my notebook away at once and
restrain the urge to inquire about anything at all. Apparently noting that he
had put the fear of god in me, Marcos assured me that I’d be perfectly fine as
long as I didn’t go poking my nose where it didn’t belong. Capurganá, after
all, was a very safe place, he said – a theme I had also heard repeatedly on
my first visit – and I could roam about at any hour of the night with no
danger of being robbed. This security, he added pointedly, was not thanks to
the police, but rather to “ _los que mandan_ ” – the ones in charge – who had
made it understood that tourists were not to be touched.

Indeed, although there was a cosmetic presence in the village of Colombian
police – whom I had observed in 2024 riding around on motorcycles and taking
selfies while migrant smuggling operations were conducted entirely out in the
open – they were definitely not the ones in charge. The ones in charge could
not be named but in fact had many [interchangeable
names](https://insightcrime.org/colombia-organized-crime-news/urabenos-
profile/): the Clan del Golfo, the Urabeños, the Ejército Gaitanista de
Colombia (the Gaitanist Army of Colombia, a reference to the politician Jorge
Eliécer Gaitán, who was assassinated in 1948), the Autodefensas Gaitanistas de
Colombia (Gaitanist Self-Defense Forces), and a revolving array of other
titles. These were the same folks who had cracked down on physical violence
against migrants on the Colombian side of the Darién Gap, which is why most
sexual and other assaults occurred on the Panamanian side. The Afro-Colombian
guide who had chaperoned my jungle incursion and exit with the two Venezuelans
had informed us that migrant “security” was such a priority for those running
the show that, for example, anyone who raped a migrant was liable to end up
dead. Naturally, this was not out of any fundamental concern for migrant
rights but rather was regarded as a better business model and a manifestation
of territorial control. The enduring paradox in Capurganá and elsewhere in
Colombia, then, is that a criminal organization imposes law and order and
metes out justice for crimes.

This is not to imply that various Colombian governments have not also
qualified as criminal organizations in their own right; ditto for their US
backers. Recall the blood-drenched reign of far-right US buddy [Álvaro
Uribe](https://colombiareports.com/the-violence-that-uribe-tried-to-cover-up-
with-fraud-and-bribery/) (2002-10), a recipient of [excessive American
aid](https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna3340831) for his ostensible war on drugs
and terror – never mind that Uribe himself had appeared on a [1991 US Defense
Intelligence Agency list](https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/document/20491-national-
security-archive-doc-01-narcotics) of the “more important Colombian narco-
terrorists contracted by the Colombian narcotic cartels.” Uribe presided over
such episodes as the [“false positives”
scandal](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2018/may/08/colombia-false-
positives-scandal-casualties-higher-thought-study), which broke in 2008 and
entailed the slaughter of thousands of civilians by members of the Colombian
army, who passed the corpses off as left-wing guerrillas and were rewarded
with bonus pay and extra holiday time while the Colombian government utilized
the ostensible battlefield successes in its appeals for yet more US aid.

As luck would have it, the Clan del Golfo was also born on Uribe’s watch – a
result of the official demobilization of the [Autodefensas Unidas de
Colombia](https://colombiareports.com/auc/) (United Self-Defense Forces of
Colombia, or AUC), the notorious paramilitary and drug trafficking
organization that had long operated in cahoots with the Colombian army and
political and business establishment and that was responsible for carrying out
all manner of massacres and other misdeeds. Carlos Castaño, who cofounded the
AUC in 1997, boasted in his biography [_Mi
Confesión_](https://www.amazon.com/Mi-Confesion-Carlos-Castano-
Secretos/dp/9580610002/) of having copied the whole “autodefensa” concept from
none other than the Israelis – because [who better than the state of
Israel](https://fair.org/home/what-we-talk-about-when-we-dont-talk-about-
genocide/) to cast mass killing and forced displacement as “self-defense”?
Castaño’s brother [Vicente](https://colombiareports.com/vicente-castano/), one
of many AUC warlords who ditched demobilization in favor of carrying on with
business, laid the foundations for the Clan del Golfo or Autodefensas
Gaitanistas de Colombia (AGC), the latter name preserving the old “self-
defense” theme. However, as scholars Reynell Badillo and Luis Fernando Trejos
Rosero point out in a [2023
paper](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/368288591_Entender_al_Clan_del_Golfo_para_entender_la_violencia_posAUC_en_Colombia_Reflexiones_sobre_la_transformacion_del_crimen_organizado_y_sus_efectos_sobre_la_paz)
on post-AUC violence in Colombia, the Clan del Golfo/AGC is not a paramilitary
organization in the traditional sense in that it is neither oriented toward
counterinsurgency nor toward cooperation with the state, with which it is
instead often in direct conflict – although there is collaboration with law
enforcement and other officials on an individual level. In certain areas of
the country controlled by the Clan del Golfo, the authors note, the group’s
power [penetrates society to such an
extent](https://voragine.co/historias/investigacion/todo-en-la-vida-tiene-
precio-el-macabro-y-millonario-negocio-del-egc-en-choco/) that even the
minutiae of daily life, as well as domestic and interpersonal matters, are
subject to AGC adjudication.

+++

Following my encounter with Marcos, I largely confined my activities in
Capurganá to wandering around trying to look like a tourist and keeping my
mouth shut. So it wasn’t my fault when on my second day in town I stumbled
upon a group of exhausted, sunscreen-slathered Venezuelans who had just been
boated in from Panama – part of the mass “[reverse
migration](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/longform/2025/6/30/coming-back-with-
nothing-inside-the-reverse-migration-away-from-the-us)” fueled by Trump’s
border shutdown and another side hustle for the Clan del Golfo. I had already
spoken with Venezuelan acquaintances of mine who had made the return trip from
Mexico and reported it to be even more harrowing and costly than the trip up,
despite the fact that the maritime route from Panama spared them from having
to recross the Darién Gap on foot. As I walked past the group in Capurganá who
were making their way to the boat ticket lines to Necoclí, one of the children
said hi to me, which I used as an excuse to strike up a conversation with the
adult family members. No sooner had they told me they were coming from the US
border than a man in a white polo shirt decided I needed to be ushered into a
separate ticket line to reconfirm my own departure for the next day.

The reconfirmation complete, I retraced my steps to the auto rickshaw stand,
where I had noticed a tent belonging to the Colombian Red Cross that
presumably served returning migrants. Thinking that perhaps at the very least
the Colombian Red Cross would be willing to talk to me, I approached the tent
but was intercepted by a young woman involved in the auto rickshaw operations,
who addressed me as though I was committing some sort of crime: “Are you
looking for something?” I went with the first innocuous response that popped
into my mind: I was looking for the path to
[Sapzurro](https://www.shutterstock.com/it/search/sapzurro), a reportedly
stunning coastal village directly on the border with Panama, which had come
highly recommended by Marcos. She pointed me in the proper direction with a
smirk and the assurance that I’d reach my destination in 90 minutes.

And so it was that I found myself on my way to Sapzurro, which turned out to
be a fairly grueling trek of much more than 90 minutes up and down a mountain
through dense and sweltering forest. I had thankfully had the foresight to
fill my backpack with cold beer – and, judging from the contents of a random
mid-jungle trash can, I had not been the only hiker to have had this idea. I
crossed paths with a smattering of other humans, one of them a gregarious
young Colombian man who spoke to me openly on a range of matters, albeit never
invoking the Clan del Golfo by name, instead relying on the pronoun “they.”
But when I later asked if he’d be amenable to being quoted anonymously in an
article – even just on the subject of the regional economic effects of
migration – he freaked out and declined. I continued on to Sapzurro, wondering
whether “security” was worth living in fear, not that “security” means much in
a country that is consistently among the
[deadliest](https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2025-12-08/its-not-
safe-to-live-here-colombia-is-deadliest-country-for-environmental-defenders)
in the world for human rights activists, environmental defenders, and trade
unionists.

At Sapzurro, I took a much-needed plunge into the magnificent aquamarine sea
and then climbed several hundred concrete steps up to the border with Panama,
where the Colombian and Panamanian flags flew side by side and no one asked
for my passport. Descending to the Panamanian village of La Miel below, I paid
a visit to the duty-free store and negotiated boat passage back to Capurganá
for around $5 – a trajectory that, according to
[certain](https://www.infobae.com/colombia/2025/03/13/disminucion-de-
migrantes-en-el-darien-afecta-la-economia-del-clan-del-golfo-en-colombia/)
media reports, could cost up to $200 for reverse migrants. The Colombian boat
captain who received my fare endeavored, to no avail, to persuade me to gift
him my Ciudad Juárez baseball cap, as well, which I had acquired during a
January 2025 trip to the Mexican border city just as Trump’s “[deportation
blitz](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2025/2/3/what-trumps-deportation-
blitz-looks-like-in-ciudad-juarez)” was kicking off. The man was a Capurganá
native, and upon hearing I was a journalist, preempted any questions I might
have with the blanket dismissal: “I don’t know anything.”

The vessel that would be transporting us for 45 minutes to Capurganá was a
rickety wooden number that would have held approximately four people
comfortably but into which ten of us had been loaded including the captain,
who thought better of it at the last minute; by this point, though, it was too
late for anyone to dismount as the waves had whipped themselves into such a
fury that we would have crashed into the dock. We thus took off frantically
out to sea for a ride that made the Necoclí-Capurganá boat look like a
soothing meditation session. I had been placed at the very front for maximum
terror and greatest impact as the boat rose almost perpendicular to the sea
and then slammed back down again. Walls of water hovered over us like cartoon
tidal waves as we lurched perilously close to rocky cliffs, and the Díaz
family from the immigration poster waved to me from my mind while I clung to
the thin wooden slat that served as my seat. I lived to tell the tale, of
course, and the following day I returned to Necoclí feeling that I had
simultaneously learned a lot and nothing at all in Capurganá.

A few months after I left Colombia, in June 2026, the _New York Times_
[reported](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/02/world/americas/us-colombia-gold-
blacklist-sanctions.html) on a request made earlier in the year by the
Colombian defense minister, who had asked the Trump administration to issue
financial sanctions against the country’s illegal gold industry, one of many
lining the pockets of the Clan del Golfo. Per the _Times_ writeup, “the
request put the Treasury Department in an unusual situation: It had, for many
years, been buying gold that originated with the very industry that it was
being asked to blacklist.” Of course, imperial hypocrisy is nothing “unusual”
– much as it may shock the US newspaper of record – as any cursory review of
the recent history of US-Colombian relations attests. In 2001, for example,
the US
[designated](https://2001-2009.state.gov/secretary/former/powell/remarks/2001/4852.htm)
the AUC as a Foreign Terrorist Organization and yet continued flinging gobs of
money at a Colombian government intimately linked to that very group. In
December 2025, the US [designated](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-
the-spokesperson/2025/12/terrorist-designations-of-clan-del-golfo) the Clan
del Golfo as a Foreign Terrorist Organization but continued buying its gold,
not to mention presiding over the criminalization of drugs and migration that
renders the organization’s trafficking activities lucrative in the first
place.

And as the whole “unusual” business proceeds as usual, there are a whole lot
of questions that should be asked.

The post [Inside the Darién
Gap](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/28/a-capurgana-diary/) appeared
first on [CounterPunch.org](https://www.counterpunch.org).
